name: Slack Pro
tagline: Run a small private team chat with channels, threads, files, and search

pricing.notes: Official Pro monthly seat price with annual billing; month-to-month is higher.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 90 days of searchable message/file history; up to 10 app integrations; 1:1 huddles; 1:1 Slack Connect

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.limits: Unlimited message/file history and integrations; group huddles; Slack Connect with up to 250 organizations
tiers.notes: A limited new-workspace promotion may discount the first 3 monthly-billed months by 50%; standard prices are recorded here.

tiers.name: Business+
tiers.limits: Unlimited history/integrations; group huddles; up to 250 Slack Connect organizations; SAML SSO and SCIM; 4-hour support response
tiers.notes: Standard prices; temporary acquisition discount excluded.

tiers.name: Enterprise+
tiers.limits: Enterprise organization, security, compliance and administration

pricing.freeTierCaps: 90-day message/file history; 10 app integrations; 1:1 huddles; 1:1 Slack Connect
pricing.hiddenCosts: A paid plan applies to the whole workspace. Active-member/fair-billing adjustments are prorated; multi-channel guests count as paid members while eligible single-channel guests can be free. The advertised 50%-for-3-months offer is temporary and only for eligible new monthly-billed workspaces.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Slack Pro, run a small private team chat with channels, threads, files, and search. The hard boundary is existing team network, integrations, push delivery, enterprise controls, and global reliability, plus network, moderation, and communication infrastructure.
coreLoopDIY: Run a small private team chat with channels, threads, file sharing, and search, and keep membership and moderation under the owner's control.
whatYouLose: existing team network, integrations, push delivery, enterprise controls, and global reliability
ongoingBurden: realtime delivery, notifications, abuse handling, search, media, permissions, mobile clients, backups, and community operations
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Slack Pro because community software is valuable when members are already there and the operator does not have to own realtime reliability and abuse response. The recurring cost buys realtime delivery, notifications, abuse handling, search, media, permissions, mobile clients, backups, and community operations, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Discourse
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source community discussion platform with strong moderation and search.

alternatives.name: Chanty Free
alternatives.desc: Five users get unlimited history, files, tasks and one-to-one calls; larger teams meet the paywall.

facts.install: Hosted signup; use Chanty's web, desktop, or mobile clients
facts.dataFormat: Chats, task records, users, and files live in Chanty's cloud; workspace data export is a Business-plan feature rather than part of the free plan.
facts.gapVsPaid: Chanty Free offers unlimited history and useful tasks, but five-member capacity, no free data export, and a far smaller integration ecosystem make it a narrow Slack Pro substitute.
facts.setupBlocker: There is no technical setup blocker, but the free workspace is limited to five members, so the sixth teammate forces a migration or payment.

alternatives.name: Element
alternatives.desc: Rooms, threads, files and encrypted calls on Matrix; the free public service avoids server duty.

facts.install: Use a free Matrix account in Element Web/mobile/desktop, or deploy Element Server Suite on your own infrastructure
facts.dataFormat: Rooms, event history, account data, and media live on the selected Matrix homeserver; encrypted-room keys remain on clients and can be backed up through Matrix's key-backup system.
facts.gapVsPaid: Element provides rooms, threads, files, calls, and encryption, but Matrix is less familiar and its workplace app and integration ecosystem is much smaller than Slack's.
facts.setupBlocker: The clean hosted path is easy, but self-hosting the current Element Server Suite means operating a Matrix homeserver and its Kubernetes/Helm-based stack.

alternatives.name: Mattermost Team Edition
alternatives.desc: Slack-shaped chat below 250 users, self-hosted; the subscription disappears and the pager appears.

facts.install: Install the official Linux binary with PostgreSQL, then configure systemd, TLS/reverse proxy, SMTP, and file storage
facts.dataFormat: Channels, posts, users, and configuration live in PostgreSQL; file attachments live in the Mattermost data directory or configured S3-compatible object storage.
facts.gapVsPaid: Mattermost Team Edition closely resembles Slack, but self-hosting adds database, email, storage, backup, upgrade, and uptime work while enterprise identity and compliance remain paid.
facts.setupBlocker: The first obstacle is a real Linux service deployment, PostgreSQL, SMTP, DNS/TLS, storage, backups, and upgrades, not an app-store install.

alternatives.name: Pumble Free
alternatives.desc: Unlimited users, channels and history with ten gigabytes total; group meetings and serious integrations still cost money.

facts.install: Hosted signup; use the browser or Pumble's desktop/mobile apps
facts.dataFormat: Messages, channels, user records, and files live in Pumble's cloud; workspace owners can export public-channel data as a ZIP with message data and file links.
facts.gapVsPaid: Pumble Free keeps unlimited users and history, but group meetings, screen sharing, integration breadth, storage, and Slack's huge app ecosystem are materially weaker.
facts.setupBlocker: There is no installation hurdle, but migration still requires inviting everyone and rebuilding channels and integrations; free exports exclude private channels and direct messages.

alternatives.name: Rocket.Chat Community
alternatives.desc: Channels, threads, files and integrations for up to a hundred concurrent users; MongoDB is the hidden teammate.

facts.install: Deploy the Community workspace with Docker Compose, Podman, or Kubernetes
facts.dataFormat: Users, rooms, messages, and most metadata live in MongoDB; uploads live on local storage or a configured object-storage backend.
facts.gapVsPaid: Rocket.Chat Community covers channels, threads, files, and integrations, but it adds MongoDB operations, a 100-concurrent-user limit, and a much smaller ecosystem than Slack.
facts.setupBlocker: A production installation requires MongoDB, DNS/TLS, email, backups, upgrades, and enough capacity planning to stay within the Community plan's 100-concurrent-user limit.

alternatives.name: Zulip
alternatives.desc: Topic-first team chat with full history and excellent search; fewer drive-by messages survive.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Pro plan and a single private community DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Slack Pro in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, WebSockets, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: run a small private team chat with channels, threads, file sharing, and search, and keep membership and moderation under the owner's control.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement spaces, channels, topics, replies, reactions, mentions, profiles, roles, and invitations.
Use WebSockets for live updates but preserve every message transactionally in PostgreSQL.
Add moderation queues, reports, blocks, rate limits, attachment limits, and an audit log.
Provide email digests, browser notifications, search, pinned content, and member export.
Add owner-controlled retention, account deletion, backup, restore, and health checks.
Ship Docker Compose with a seeded demo, migrations, and an emergency admin command.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out public-network discovery and existing member liquidity.
Deliberately leave out production voice or video rooms.
Deliberately leave out native mobile applications, enterprise SSO, and 24-hour abuse operations.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
